title: 2023 budget preview, user fees and utility rates
subtitle: Planning fee deferral, pre-approved capital projects, community agreements, development charge hearings and a lower natural gas supply rate.
overview: The committee received the first overview of the 2023 budget. Staff proposed a 4.8% overall tax increase and a 4.5% water utility increase. The tax increase is about $56 a year for the average household, and the water increase is about $42. Roughly $1.5 million was left unallocated for Council priorities. Detailed budget review is set for January.

The committee recommended most 2023 user fees but deferred planning fees and two new engineering fees to the December 19 Council meeting. Councillors raised concerns about housing affordability and asked to see examples of the cost to applicants. It also recommended the 2023 water utility rates {{vote:m7}}. For natural gas, it recommended lowering the supply rate while delivery rates rise, so the average residential customer would pay about $81 more a year.

The committee also recommended pre-approving 2023 capital projects so tenders can go out early, and moving funding for two community organizations from the grant program to the operating budget. It recommended a Fergus Avenue contract increase and a process for development charge dispute hearings.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended approving the 2023 user fee schedule, except planning fees (lines 232 to 319) and two engineering fees (lines 229 and 230), which were deferred to the December 19 Council meeting.
The committee recommended approving the proposed 2023 water, sanitary and stormwater rates, a combined 4.5% increase of about $42 a year for the average household.
The committee recommended cutting the supply rate to 20.85 cents per cubic metre from 21.45, approving the proposed delivery rates, and reviewing the supply rate quarterly.
The committee recommended that Council pre-approve the listed capital projects for procurement before the 2023 budget is passed.
The committee recommended that it be delegated Council's authority to hear section 20 Development Charges Act complaints, following the process in the staff report.
The committee recommended moving $158,621 from the Tier 1 grant program to the operating budget and authorizing a funding agreement every two years for food programs at City facilities.
The committee recommended a five-year funding agreement extension with the centre and moving $55,403 from the Tier 1 grant program to the operating budget.
The committee recommended increasing the Steed and Evans Limited purchase order by $90,000, funded from an existing project surplus.

debate: On moving agency funding out of the grant stream, staff said these are services the City outsources rather than grants. Operating-budget funding is more predictable, and the agencies no longer reapply each year.

On pre-approving capital projects, a councillor asked why the projects were not reviewed within the full budget. Staff said early tenders draw more bids and better prices, that prices are expected to keep rising, and that an election year delays budget approval. Any savings return to reserves.

On planning fees, several councillors worried about affordability and mixed messages given the province's Bill 23. They noted that homebuyers, not developers, ultimately bear the cost. Staff said a consultant's study tied fees to staff effort, builders' groups supported cost recovery, and small-scale applications stay near a 4% increase. The fee study was to be shared with Council.

On user fees, a councillor asked about seniors' recreation fees and whether to lower fees for electric vehicle charging, green burial and downtown parking. Staff pointed to a budget issue paper with targeted reductions and the leisure access subsidy. They said the parking enterprise is already losing money, and that fees should keep pace with inflation to avoid shifting costs to property taxes.

On water rates, a councillor asked whether the increase could be lowered or deferred because households are struggling. Staff said maintenance was deferred during the pandemic years, reserves are running low, and the stormwater increase is driven by a federal grant program whose costs have risen. A deferral would require a larger increase later. The deferral request was withdrawn.
